opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people, when they hear "AGI," imagine there's going to be some single test, like a finish line, where the model crosses it and we all agree. I don't really think about it that way. For me, the more useful question is whether models can do the kinds of economically valuable work that people actually do, and do it well enough that you'd trust the output.

A lot of the classic benchmarks we've used were really academic in flavor: exam-style questions, competition math, multiple-choice knowledge tests. Those were great for a while, but models have gotten so good that many of them are saturated, and even when they aren't, doing well on an exam isn't the same as being able to do someone's job. So a big part of how I think about it is grounding evaluation in real tasks. You go to experienced professionals across a bunch of occupations, like lawyers, nurses, engineers, and financial analysts, and ask them for representative work they actually do: a memo, a spreadsheet model, a care plan, a design document. Then you have the model do the same task and have other experts compare the outputs blind, without knowing which came from a human and which came from the model.

That gives you something much more concrete than "is it smart?" You can ask: across all these occupations, how often is the model's work as good as or better than an expert's? Where does it fall short? Is it formatting, is it following instructions, is it subtle domain mistakes? And you can track that over time, which tells you a lot about the trajectory.

Even that is only part of the picture, though. Real jobs aren't one-shot tasks. They involve long time horizons, ambiguity, gathering context, working with other people, iterating on feedback. So I think evaluations have to keep moving toward longer, messier, more agentic work. And honestly, I think the clearest signal of AGI won't come from a single eval score. It will come from seeing models meaningfully contribute across a wide range of the work people do, and eventually help with things like scientific discovery. Our job on the evals side is to measure that progress as faithfully as we can so we're not surprised by it.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the Turing test or say that passing it attracted little attention.

r002.rationale: It frames economically valuable work as a useful basis for evaluation, but does not clearly propose performing most such work; it refers instead to representative tasks across occupations and a wide range of work.

r003.rationale: It rejects the idea of a single AGI finish-line test that everyone would agree on, conveying that there may be disagreement about when models reach AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've come to think "has it reached AGI" is the wrong shape of question. It treats AGI like a line you cross, and in practice what we see is much more jagged than that. A model can be superhuman at one thing and still fail at something a reasonably competent person would find easy. So instead of one threshold, I think about a portfolio of capabilities and ask: on which real tasks, done the way real people actually do them, is the model at or above the level of a competent professional?

That framing pushes you toward evals that look like work rather than like trivia. The benchmarks that got us here, multiple-choice knowledge tests, competition math, those are saturating, and saturation on a test tells you much less than you'd hope. What I care about now is: can the model do a multi-hour task end to end? Can it work in a messy environment where the instructions are ambiguous, the data is incomplete, and it has to notice when it's wrong and recover? Can it produce something a domain expert would accept as a deliverable, not just an answer that pattern-matches to one? We try to build evals where the grading is done by people who actually do that job, against outputs that are judged the way their own work would be judged.

There's also a measurement problem that's easy to underrate. Any single eval is a proxy, and proxies get gamed, sometimes deliberately through contamination, sometimes just because the field optimizes toward whatever's being measured. So I put a lot of weight on held-out tasks, on fresh tasks that didn't exist when the model was trained, and on looking at the distribution of failures rather than the headline number. A ninety percent score where the ten percent failures are catastrophic means something very different from one where they're minor.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that economic and real-world impact is ultimately the ground truth. If a model can autonomously do a meaningful fraction of the tasks that make up a job, that matters more than any benchmark. So I think of AGI less as a verdict we declare and more as a dial we keep measuring, carefully, with evals that stay honest about what they can and can't tell us.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the Turing test or the attention its passage received.

r002.rationale: It says economic impact is a ground truth and discusses a meaningful fraction of job tasks, but does not propose performing most economically valuable work as the AGI test.

r003.rationale: It rejects a single threshold and describes AGI as a dial, but does not anticipate disagreement over the precise point at which models reach AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to make that question more concrete: what would a model actually need to be able to do for us to consider it AGI? There’s a big difference between answering a difficult question on a benchmark and reliably carrying out a complex task in the real world.

So I’d want to look at a range of capabilities. Can it learn something new? Can it apply what it’s learned in an unfamiliar situation? Can it work through a longer task, recognize when it’s made a mistake, and recover? And how much human guidance does it need along the way?

I wouldn’t expect a single score to settle the question. I’d want evidence across different tasks and environments, with particular attention to where the model still fails. That gives us a more useful picture than just asking whether it’s crossed one threshold.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the Turing test or how much attention models passing it received.

r002.rationale: It discusses varied capabilities and real-world tasks, but does not propose performing most economically valuable work as the AGI test.

r003.rationale: It says no single score would settle the question, but does not anticipate disagreement about the precise point at which AI reaches AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that AGI isn’t something we have a single, agreed-upon test for. So I’d start by making the question more concrete: What capabilities are we looking for, and what evidence would convince us that the model has them?

You’d want to evaluate breadth—can it perform well across very different kinds of tasks? But also generalization: when you give it a problem that’s genuinely new, can it learn what it needs, adapt, and make progress? And then there’s reliability. Getting something right once is very different from being able to do it consistently, especially over a long task where mistakes can compound.

So I’d think about it as a collection of evidence, including performance on realistic tasks, rather than one benchmark score. And I’d separate the capability question from the safety question. Evidence that a model is broadly capable doesn’t, by itself, establish that we can deploy it safely.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Turing tests or the attention they received.

r002.rationale: It discusses broad capabilities and realistic tasks, but does not propose performing most economically valuable work as the AGI test.

r003.rationale: Saying there is no single agreed-upon test for AGI communicates that people may disagree about how to determine when a model has reached it.
